description: In his first year over Babylon, Cyrus of Persia decrees that the temple in Jerusalem be rebuilt and lets the exiles go home (2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–4). The text dates it only to Cyrus's first year. This timeline's chronology puts it in 536 BC; most modern scholars date the decree to 538 BC.
Some 42,000 exiles return to Judah under Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Joshua) the high priest, bringing back the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off (Ezra 1:5–2:70).

In the second year after their return, Zerubbabel and Joshua lay the foundation of the new temple; the people shout for joy while the old men who had seen Solomon's temple weep (Ezra 3:8–13). Opposition halts the work until the second year of Darius (Ezra 4:24), and the house is finished in his sixth year (Ezra 6:15).
Stirred by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, Zerubbabel and Joshua take up the work on the temple again in the second year of Darius (Ezra 5:1–2; Haggai 1:1, 14–15).
The temple is finished on the third day of Adar in the sixth year of Darius (Ezra 6:15). It is dedicated with sacrifices, and the returned exiles keep the Passover (Ezra 6:16–22).

Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, is chosen as queen by King Ahasuerus at Shushan (Susa) in the tenth month of his seventh year (Esther 2:7, 16–17). This timeline follows Theographic, which takes Ahasuerus to be Darius I and so dates this to 515 BC; most scholars identify him with Xerxes I, which gives 479 BC.

In Ahasuerus's twelfth year Haman casts lots to fix a day to destroy the Jews, and the king seals his decree (Esther 3). Mordecai mourns and charges Esther to plead with the king for her people (Esther 4).
At her banquet Esther exposes Haman's plot to the king, and Haman is hanged on the gallows he had made for Mordecai. His house is given to Esther (Esther 7:1–8:2).

A second decree lets the Jews defend themselves. On the thirteenth of Adar, the day Haman had set, they overcome their enemies, and Mordecai and Esther establish the feast of Purim to remember it (Esther 8–9).

Ezra the scribe leads a second company of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem with the backing of Artaxerxes, to teach the law and set the temple's worship in order. Ezra 7:7–9 dates the journey to the seventh year of Artaxerxes: 467 BC on this timeline's chronology, 458 BC in most others.

At Shushan, in the month Chisleu of Artaxerxes' twentieth year, Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, hears from Hanani that Jerusalem's wall is broken down and its gates burned. He weeps, fasts and prays (Nehemiah 1).

Sent as governor in Artaxerxes' twentieth year (Nehemiah 2:1), Nehemiah has the people rebuild Jerusalem's wall gate by gate. Despite the opposition of Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem, it is finished in 52 days (Nehemiah 3–6; 6:15). This timeline's chronology puts this in 454 BC; most others give 445 BC.

name: Ezra Reads the Law
description: In the seventh month, once the wall is finished, Ezra reads the book of the law of Moses to the people gathered in Jerusalem, with Nehemiah the governor beside him. They weep, then keep the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8). Dated to the same year as the wall.

name: Nehemiah's Second Term as Governor
description: After returning to Artaxerxes in the king's thirty-second year (Nehemiah 13:6), Nehemiah comes back to Jerusalem. He throws Tobiah out of the temple's storerooms and restores the tithes, the Sabbath, and the ban on foreign marriages (Nehemiah 13). This is the last dated event in the Old Testament: 442 BC on this timeline's chronology, about 432 BC in most others.

name: Dedication of the Wall of Jerusalem
description: With the wall finished, the Levites and singers are gathered to Jerusalem, and two great choirs go round on the wall in procession, one with Ezra the scribe at its head and the other with Nehemiah behind it, meeting at the house of God (Nehemiah 12:27–43). The text doesn't date it; it follows the wall's completion in Artaxerxes' twentieth year (Nehemiah 2:1; 6:15), so it's placed in the same year as the wall, 454 BC on this timeline's chronology.
